idiom_name: hand-written gate over threading.Condition (reader count + writer flag); readerwriterlock package packages the same structure
implementation_notes: The Python stdlib has no reader-writer lock: threading ships Lock, RLock, Semaphore and Condition, so the gate is built from a Condition plus a reader count and an active-writer flag - re-check the predicate in a while loop, notify_all when the last reader leaves or when a writer releases. The third-party readerwriterlock package wraps exactly that structure. Because CPython's GIL serialises bytecode, a pure-Python reader-writer lock usually loses to a plain Lock for CPU-bound readers; it pays off when read sections block on I/O (the GIL is released there) and under free-threaded 3.13+ builds, and it is a poor substitute for immutable snapshots or concurrent.futures in massively read-dominated code.
pitfalls: A wait without a while-loop re-check breaks under spurious wakeups and notification storms; the predicate must be re-evaluated after every wake.
notify() instead of notify_all() loses wakeups when readers and writers share one condition variable - the wrong side is woken and the notification is gone.
Running the protected function while holding the condition's lock serialises everything again; the gate must release before calling user code.
Under the GIL the pure-Python gate usually costs more than a plain Lock for short CPU-bound reads; measure, and prefer immutable snapshots or a single-owner queue where reads dominate massively.
